title: Scope and definitions: Victorian barriers for spas and pools
audience: Pool and spa service workers, installers and supervisors working in Victoria. The rules are Victorian.
learningOutcomes: List the pool and spa types that the Victorian note brings within scope.
Identify the water depths and features that fall outside the barrier rule.
Define the terms used in the note: swimming pool area (this lesson's pool zone), barrier height, non-climbable zone, boundary barrier and young child.

instruction.heading: Who the note is written for
instruction.body: Victorian rule (VBA Building Practice Note SP 02, Version 3, 26 September 2023). The note is written for designers, builders, building surveyors, owners, plumbers and electricians, and it covers barriers for indoor and outdoor pools.

instruction.heading: Features outside the barrier rule
instruction.body: A pool, under the note, is an excavation or structure able to hold water deeper than 300 mm and used mainly for swimming, wading, paddling, bathing or similar activities. A shallower feature therefore falls outside the barrier rule. The VBA consumer page on pool safety barriers also exempts bird baths, fountains, water tanks, fish ponds, dams, and personal-hygiene baths or indoor spas emptied after each use. Judge each feature by its depth and how it is used, not by what it is called.

instruction.heading: Terms used in the note
instruction.body: Barrier height is measured at right angles to the finished ground level (FGL). A boundary barrier separates two neighbouring properties. A non-climbable zone is the strip on and beside a barrier, running its full length including any gate, meant to stop young children from climbing it. The note calls the enclosed area the swimming pool area: the area containing the pool or spa, enclosed by a barrier. The note does not define pool zone, so this lesson uses that term for the same area. A young child is a child under five. A spa counts as part of the pool.

instruction.heading: The whole lot is not the pool zone
instruction.body: The pool area must be a separate area enclosed by a barrier. Enclosing the whole property does not satisfy the barrier requirement, and access must not be directly available through a building door.

instruction.heading: Standards that sit behind the rule
instruction.body: The note names AS 1926.1-2012 as the barrier standard and refers to NCC 2022. The 2012 edition of AS 1926.1 was not read for this lesson, so the standard is cited by name only, and its current edition has not yet been confirmed. Check with the relevant regulator before relying on this point.

procedure: Confirm the feature is a pool or a spa, and note its deepest water level.
Check the feature against the features outside the rule, and record the basis for any exclusion.
Confirm the building class and whether the pool serves a children's service.
Identify the pool zone as its own enclosed area, and record how it is closed off.
Record the state as Victoria, and leave out any point you have not confirmed.

workedExamples.situation: A homeowner in Melbourne has a spa that is drained after each use and sits in the ensuite. A second homeowner has a 400 mm deep plunge pool in the back yard.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Which feature needs a safety barrier, and why?
workedExamples.reasoning: The ensuite spa is a tub used for washing and drained after use, so the barrier rule does not apply to it. The plunge pool is deeper than 300 mm, so a complying barrier is needed. Record the reasoning and confirm the barrier with the building surveyor.

equipmentAndPpe: Copy of the permit, if one exists

commonErrors.error: Excluding a feature because of its name, such as calling a plunge pool a bath.
commonErrors.prevention: Classify by use, water depth and how the feature is emptied.

commonErrors.error: Treating the whole yard as the pool zone.
commonErrors.prevention: The pool zone is its own enclosed area around the water.

commonErrors.error: Assuming the Victorian rules apply in another state.
commonErrors.prevention: Leave out every requirement for other states and territories until it is checked.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Water deeper than 300 mm can drown a small child. A complying barrier is needed once the feature reaches that depth; this lesson sets the scope only.
Building work on pools and barriers in Victoria needs a permit, and the work must be done by registered or authorised people. This lesson does not grant a licence or permit.

qualityStandard: Each feature is recorded as inside or outside the rule, with the reason.
The pool zone is recorded as its own enclosed area.
Every requirement outside Victoria, and the current standard edition, is left out until checked.
documentationEvidence: Scope record showing feature type, depth, use, building class and reason for any exclusion
Record of the state and any items still to be checked
summary: Pools and spas deeper than 300 mm need a complying barrier in Victoria.
The pool zone is its own enclosed area, not the whole lot.
A young child is under five. The rules are Victorian.

knowledgeChecks.question: Under the Victorian note, at what water depth does a pool generally need a complying safety barrier?
Which feature is left out of the barrier rule in the note?
How does the note's definitions section describe the swimming pool area?
options: The whole lot, including the car park and the garden
The walled-off area around the water, bounded by the barrier
Any area within 10 m of the water and the path to the gate
The area under the building and the car park beside it

sourceReferences: Victorian Building Authority, Building Practice Note SP 02, Swimming pool barriers and other requirements (Version 3, 26 September 2023), pool definition, barrier-height, non-climbable zone and boundary sections; rights: user-held; reworded (no copying)

Priority: official Victorian Building Authority source. It overrides other pool sources on the points it covers, for Victoria only. Dated: 26 September 2023 (Version 3); read through a summary tool on 2026-11-03. Victorian requirement. UNCONFIRMED for other states and territories, and the current edition of AS 1926.1 is UNCONFIRMED.
UNCONFIRMED: Victorian scope applied to other states and territories; current edition of AS 1926.1 (named only, text not read).

officialReferences.title: Victorian Building Authority: Pool safety barriers (consumers)
officialReferences.pageDate: no single publication date; checklists are keyed to installation dates (before 8 April 1991; 8 April 1991 to 30 April 2010; from 1 May 2010)
officialReferences.covers: Read through a summary tool (WebFetch): pools and spas that can hold water deeper than 300 mm need a compliant barrier; exemptions named on the page include bird baths, fountains, water tanks, fish ponds, dams, personal-hygiene baths or indoor spas emptied after each use, and pools that cannot exceed 300 mm; new pools in Victoria fall under the Building Regulations 2018, with work done by a registered builder or an owner-builder with a certificate of consent; barriers must meet AS1926.1-2012 as stated on the page. The page does not mention a non-climbable zone, so that definition is not confirmed by this source.

officialReferences.title: Building Practice Note SP 02, Swimming pool barriers and other requirements (Victorian Building Authority), Version 3
officialReferences.covers: Victorian Building Authority Building Practice Note SP 02, Version 3, published 26 September 2023 (no review date shown). The pool definition covers any excavation or structure, including a spa or relocatable structure, capable of containing water, and refers to a depth of 300 mm. Barrier height is measured perpendicular to the finished ground level. The page defines the non-climbable zone and the young child as a child under five. The outdoor swimming pool area must be a separate area enclosed by a barrier. Publisher: Victorian Building Authority.
